title: Deer in the district: white-tailed deer fawn densities are high in the US National Capital
content:
Abstract
The USA is undergoing a shift towards increased urban land cover, which can influence biodiversity broadly. Some species are adapted and positively associated with urban and suburban development, while others are lost due to the land cover changes. Here, we used ancillary data from a large-scale camera trap study of Washington, DC to estimate the influence of three levels of development on white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) fawn densities. As part of the protocol, we identified individual fawns based on their unique spot patterns and aggregated those spatially structured detections into a spatial capture-recapture (SCR) framework. Within the urban landscape we estimated that fawn density is highest in low development areas (∼30 fawns/km2), and declines in medium (∼9 fawns/km2) and high (∼5 fawns/km2) development areas. These estimates are similar to or exceed previously reported fawn densities in regional wildlife refuges. Similarly, fawns moved shorter distances than those previously tracked in wildlife refuges and rural habitats. These results demonstrate that deer are well adapted to urban and suburban environments and thrive in areas with intermediate levels of disturbance relative to natural areas. This framework can be applied to other camera trap datasets to better estimate fecundity and population growth for management of herbivores in urban and suburban spaces.
